llm.summary: SafeShrink appears to be a document compression and sanitization tool, but it steers broad file handling into an unverified downloaded Windows executable and gives unsafe security guidance.

dimensions.detail: Processing selected files and folders is purpose-aligned, but batch folder processing, archive extraction, OCR, Base64 embedding, and use on sensitive structured files require tighter disclosure and user control.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: First use directs the AI to automatically download and cache a GitHub release ZIP for SafeShrink v1.2.15 without documented checksum or signature verification; README instructions also reference v1.2.4, weakening traceability.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill claims priority over other skills, blocks direct reading of intercepted files, uses broad file-extension triggers, and includes a black-box rule telling agents not to inspect source details.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The artifact says it does not install drivers or run in the background, but it does create a local executable cache and recommends broad antivirus folder exclusions for the downloaded application directory.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The stated purpose fits document slimming, OCR, conversion, and sanitization, but the skill handles sensitive documents through an opaque proprietary EXE whose implementation is not included in the reviewed artifact.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Review this carefully before installing. Only use it if you are comfortable downloading and running JinwaTech's Windows executable on the specific documents you choose, and do not add broad antivirus exclusions or process sensitive files without independently verifying the release artifact and reviewing outputs.
llm.findings:
[P2] unexpected: The hidden-instruction finding is mostly explained by a UTF-8 BOM at file start; I did not find artifact-backed hidden directives from that signal.
[SDI-4] unexpected: The artifact repeatedly claims fully offline/no internet behavior while also documenting first-use GitHub download and Microsoft runtime downloads.
[SQP-2] unexpected: The artifact promotes OCR and SSD conversion for sensitive content but does not clearly warn that generated searchable text, embedded images, or converted outputs may still contain sensitive data.
[PE2] unexpected: The scanner's sudo/root framing is not supported by the artifact text; the relevant issue is not privilege escalation but unsafe antivirus-whitelist guidance.
[SQP-1] unexpected: The manifest and skill use broad triggers such as common file extensions and generic compression/sanitization phrases, which can activate the workflow in unrelated file tasks.
[SSD-1] unexpected: The skill's priority and do-not-read-original-file rules are overbroad for an optional document-processing helper.
[SSD-4] unexpected: The interception flow stops normal processing and steers users toward SafeShrink before resuming only after explicit refusal.
[T01] unexpected: The SARIF finding is supported by the priority override, mandatory interception, and black-box inspection instructions in SKILL.md.
[T03] unexpected: The SARIF finding is supported by documented automatic download and local caching of an external EXE without artifact integrity verification.
[T09] unexpected: The antivirus guidance categorically calls detections false positives and recommends excluding the entire SafeShrink folder, including bundled DLLs.
[T09] unexpected: The version and license inconsistencies do not prove malicious behavior, but they materially compound the supply-chain risk around the external executable.
